newsitem.title: UK: Brent crude loses ground with closed U.S. arb.
newsitem.headline: Brent crude loses ground with closed U.S. arb.

text.p: North Sea benchmark crude Brent slipped further on Wednesday as the market was weighed down by June barrels seeking homes with a closing arbitrage to the United States, traders said. No further physical deals were reported after a June 10-12 Brent changed hands early at a 48 cents discount to July Brent - or four cents below the lowest deal a day earlier. "The market is in contango. It is under pressure from the plenty of avails and arbitrage to the U.S. is shut," one North Sea trader said.

"In July, some of the maintenance programmes will be over so production will be increasing, which is another bearish factor," he added. But another trader, dismissing what he called an "allegedly closed arbitrage" was having a major impact on the market, said.

"The market is a little bit more contagoed than it was because people are making Brent weaker and weaker and that has brought the differentials down". Traders said that bearish U.S. inventory data showing a crude build last week was making transatlantic sales very difficult. Other North Sea grades were also looking weaker after two deals on Tuesday.

A late June Forties changed hands at Dated Brent +25 cents -- 10 cents down on last done -- and a June 24-26 Statfjord also fetched a 25 cents premium to Dated Brent, or three cents lower than another deal that day.

But some sellers were optmistic with one Norwegian producer saying that "absolute prices are coming down and margins are improving so the market should pick up". On cash, July Brent was five cents down at $18.85 a barrel while July outrights traded at $18.88 and $18.89.

Brent intermonth spreads were largely unchanged over the day, with Jul/Aug trading twice at -17 cents after an earlier trade at one cent lower. Prompt Brent CFDs slipped further with this week's talked four cents weaker at July Brent -50/-43 cents and June 9-13 talked one or two cents weaker after trading twice at July Brent -42 cents. The only Brent cargo turning wet on Wednesday went unclaimed and was clocked to Texaco. The cargo is due to load June 19-21. In the Mediterranean, Russian Urals found some short-term strength after two large cargoes traded on Tuesday at Dated Brent -$1.33 and $1.31 c+f Med.
Only two large cargoes were left on offer and offers climbed to Dated Brent -$1.25/$1.30 basis cif Genoa.
Traders put the more bullish sentiment down to an improvement in refining margins following benchmark Brent's sharp dip on Tuesday.
Longer-term, Iraqi crude exports under the renewed United Nations oil-for-food deal were likely to weaken sour crude markets, traders said.
The U.N. Security Council on Tuesday voted to extend the agreement with Iraq for a further six months.
"I see the market weakening as soon as an official announcement is made," said one trader earlier in the day.
From June 8, Iraq will be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food, medicine and other goods.
But traders said that fresh exports are unlikely to start flowing until the third decade of June.
The West African market was seen poorly supported with full-to-the-brim storage tanks curbing demand from U.S. Gulf coast refiners.
Meanwhile a Brent/Dubai spread approaching +$1.00 was stifling buying interest from the Far East, traders said.
At least half a dozen June cargoes are still left unsold, with a Brass River loading June 22-24 trading on Tuesday at a distressed Dated Brent +33 cents.
